fm_circular_horizontal.description: Convert angular speed and period, identify the inward force and check friction and contact on horizontal paths.

sections.title: How are linear speed, angular speed and period related?
sections.label: Convert the rates
sections.intro: One complete revolution is two pi radians. Period is the time per revolution.

blocks.html: Use \(\omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}\) and \(v=r\omega\).

blocks.title: Convert revolutions into period and speed
blocks.prompt: A marker at radius \(1\) metres completes \(60\) revolutions per minute. Find the period in seconds and the exact speed.
blocks.hint: Convert minutes to seconds before finding the duration of one revolution.
blocks.solution:
A revolution takes \(1\) seconds. The angular speed is \(2 \pi\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).

Multiply angular speed by its radius. The period is \(1\) seconds and the speed is \(2 \pi\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: Convert revolutions per minute before using seconds.

sections.title: Why is there acceleration at constant speed?
sections.label: Resolve towards the centre
sections.intro: The direction of the velocity changes continually. The instantaneous acceleration needed for uniform circular motion is radial and inward.

blocks.html: \(a_r=\frac{v^2}{r}=r\omega^2\). The combined inward component of the real forces equals \(ma_r\).

figure.alt: At P on a circle the acceleration points to centre O while velocity is tangent.
figure.caption: The radial direction points to the centre. The tangent velocity points along the motion.

blocks.title: Use the radial force equation
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(5\) kilograms moves at speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) in a horizontal circle of radius \(2\) metres. Find the magnitude of acceleration and the inward resultant force.
blocks.hint: Centripetal force is the combined inward effect of actual forces.
blocks.solution:
The velocity changes direction. Its acceleration is inward, with magnitude \(\frac{v^2}{r}\).

The acceleration is \(\frac{25}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Multiply by mass; the inward resultant is \(\frac{125}{2}\,\mathrm N\).

blocks.html: Do not draw ‘centripetal force’ as an extra force.

sections.title: How can tension reveal speed?
sections.label: Use the horizontal tension
sections.intro: On a smooth horizontal table, the normal balances weight. For a taut horizontal string fixed at the centre, tension supplies the radial force.

blocks.html: Write \(T=\frac{mv^2}{r}\) when it is the only radial force.

blocks.title: Use the radial force equation
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(5\) kilograms moves on a smooth horizontal table, attached to a taut string of length \(2\) metres fixed at the centre. The tension is \(\frac{125}{2}\,\mathrm N\). Find the exact speed.
blocks.hint: Centripetal force is the combined inward effect of actual forces.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal radial resultant is the tension. Set it equal to \(\frac{mv^2}{r}\).

Use a positive square root. The speed is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: Use radius, not diameter, in the denominator.

blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(9\) kilograms moves on a smooth horizontal table, attached to a taut string of length \(\frac{8}{3}\) metres fixed at the centre. The tension is \(\frac{1323}{8}\,\mathrm N\). Find the exact speed.

sections.title: Can static friction provide the whole inward force?
sections.label: Check the friction capacity
sections.intro: A body that rotates with a horizontal disc needs inward static friction even if it is at rest relative to the disc.

blocks.html: Demand is \(mr\omega^2\) and capacity is \(\mu mg\) for this level arrangement.

blocks.title: Find the minimum friction on a turntable
blocks.prompt: A token remains fixed relative to a rough horizontal disc at radius \(\frac{3}{4}\) metres, rotating at \(1\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Find the least coefficient of static friction. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
blocks.hint: Balance weight vertically, then use friction as the inward force.
blocks.solution:
The vertical normal reaction equals weight. Static friction is the only inward horizontal force.

Its required magnitude is \(mr\omega^2\). At the minimum coefficient, the limit is equal to the demand.

Divide by \(mg\) to get coefficient \(\frac{3}{40}\).

blocks.html: Do not assume the friction is limiting before the threshold is requested.

sections.title: Which contact points towards the centre?
sections.label: Identify the real contact forces
sections.intro: A smooth upright wall has a horizontal contact reaction. A horizontal surface underneath has a separate vertical reaction.

blocks.html: Resolve along the horizontal radius and vertically as two different equations.

blocks.title: Identify the inward force at a circular wall
blocks.prompt: A small particle on a smooth horizontal platform is kept in a circle by contact with the inside face of a smooth vertical circular wall. Mass is \(\frac{5}{3}\) kilograms, radius \(3\) metres, and speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the wall force and explain its direction. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
blocks.hint: Separate the vertical reaction of the platform from horizontal contact with the upright wall.
blocks.solution:
The wall’s force is perpendicular to the wall and points horizontally towards the centre. The platform's reaction balances the weight.

The inward radial resultant is the wall's normal force. Its magnitude is \(\frac{125}{9}\,\mathrm N\).

blocks.html: Only the components towards or away from the centre enter the radial equation.

related.title: Conical pendulums, linked strings and elastic constraints

fm_circular_conical.description: Use geometry, vertical balance and radial dynamics to find radii, tensions and angular speeds.

sections.title: Which radius describes the pendulum's circle?
sections.label: Read the conical geometry
sections.intro: The string sweeps a cone while the mass moves in a horizontal circle. The slant string is not the horizontal radius.

blocks.html: With \(\theta\) to the vertical and string length \(L\), \(r=L\sin\theta\), \(T\cos\theta=mg\) and \(T\sin\theta=mr\omega^2\).

figure.alt: The slant string from A to P meets a dashed vertical axis and a horizontal circular radius.
figure.caption: The slant length is greater than the horizontal radius. Resolve tension relative to the vertical.

blocks.title: Resolve the conical pendulum
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(\frac{3}{2}\) kilograms is attached to a light inextensible string of length \(2\) metres and moves in a horizontal circle. The sine of its angle to the vertical is \(\frac{3}{5}\). Find the radius and tension. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
blocks.hint: Use the horizontal circular radius, rather than the slant length, in the acceleration.
blocks.solution:
Use \(r=L\sin\theta\). The inclined tension has upward component \(T\cos\theta\) and inward component \(T\sin\theta\).

Vertical balance and the radial equation give \(T\cos\theta=mg\) and \(T\sin\theta=mr\omega^2\), so \(L\omega^2\cos\theta=g\).

The cosine is \(\frac{4}{5}\), radius \(\frac{6}{5}\) metres and tension \(\frac{75}{4}\,\mathrm N\).

blocks.html: Use cosine for the vertical component when the angle is measured from vertical.

sections.title: How does angular speed reveal the cone angle?
sections.label: Eliminate the tension
sections.intro: Substitute the geometric radius into the radial equation. For a non-zero radius the sine factors cancel.

blocks.html: Combine the equations to obtain \(L\omega^2\cos\theta=g\).

blocks.title: Resolve the conical pendulum
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass \(\frac{3}{2}\) kilograms is attached to a light inextensible string of length \(2\) metres and moves in a horizontal circle. Angular speed is \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Find the cosine of the angle to the vertical and the radius. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
blocks.hint: Use the horizontal circular radius, rather than the slant length, in the acceleration.
blocks.solution:
Use \(r=L\sin\theta\). The inclined tension has upward component \(T\cos\theta\) and inward component \(T\sin\theta\).

Vertical balance and the radial equation give \(T\cos\theta=mg\) and \(T\sin\theta=mr\omega^2\), so \(L\omega^2\cos\theta=g\).

The cosine is \(\frac{4}{5}\), radius \(\frac{6}{5}\) metres and tension \(\frac{75}{4}\,\mathrm N\).

blocks.html: A cosine outside the valid interval rules out the proposed conical motion.

sections.title: How do two strings contribute to the turn?
sections.label: Add and subtract components
sections.intro: In the symmetrical two-string arrangement, both tensions pull inward, but their vertical components oppose each other.

blocks.html: Vertical balance fixes the difference of the tensions, and radial demand fixes their sum.

blocks.title: Resolve both string tensions
blocks.prompt: Two equal light strings of length \(3\) metres connect a mass of \(3\) kilograms to fixed points directly above and below the circle's centre, symmetrically spaced. Each string makes an acute angle having cosine \(\frac{4}{5}\) with the vertical. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The angular speed is \(\frac{7 \sqrt{6}}{6}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Find both tensions.
blocks.hint: Add the inward components and subtract the vertical components.
blocks.solution:
The upper string pulls partly up, while the lower one pulls partly down. Both pull towards the axis in the horizontal direction.

Vertical balance fixes \(T_U-T_L\), while the required radial force fixes \(T_U+T_L\).

Solving gives upper tension \(\frac{111}{2}\,\mathrm N\) and lower tension \(18\,\mathrm N\). Both are positive.

blocks.html: A string with negative tension cannot provide the assumed force.

blocks.title: Resolve both string tensions
blocks.prompt: Two equal light strings of length \(4\) metres connect a mass of \(5\) kilograms to fixed points directly above and below the circle's centre, symmetrically spaced. Each string makes an acute angle having cosine \(\frac{4}{5}\) with the vertical. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The angular speed is \(\frac{\sqrt{146}}{4}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Find both tensions.
blocks.hint: Add the inward components and subtract the vertical components.
blocks.solution:
The upper string pulls partly up, while the lower one pulls partly down. Both pull towards the axis in the horizontal direction.

Vertical balance fixes \(T_U-T_L\), while the required radial force fixes \(T_U+T_L\).

Solving gives upper tension \(\frac{245}{2}\,\mathrm N\) and lower tension \(60\,\mathrm N\). Both are positive.

sections.title: At what angular speed can both strings stay straight?
sections.label: Check non-negative tensions
sections.intro: Vertical balance sets the difference of the two tensions. When the radial demand is too low, the required lower tension becomes negative.

blocks.html: Use zero lower tension at the boundary. Strictly positive tension requires a higher angular speed.

blocks.title: Resolve both string tensions
blocks.prompt: Two equal light strings of length \(3\) metres connect a mass of \(3\) kilograms to fixed points directly above and below the circle's centre, symmetrically spaced. Each string makes an acute angle having cosine \(\frac{4}{5}\) with the vertical. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the minimum angular speed for the model with both strings straight and each tension non-negative.
blocks.hint: Add the inward components and subtract the vertical components.
blocks.solution:
Both tensions pull radially inwards. The upper one contributes upwards, the lower one downwards.

Write \((T_U+T_L)\sin\theta=mr\omega^2\) and \((T_U-T_L)\cos\theta=mg\).

At the threshold \(T_L=0\), so angular speed is \(\frac{5 \sqrt{6}}{6}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).

blocks.html: The higher string need not be at its limiting tension at this event.

sections.title: What length appears in an elastic conical pendulum?
sections.label: Solve for the stretched string
sections.intro: A Hookean string has a natural length and a separate stretched length. Use the latter to draw the circular geometry.

blocks.html: Use \(T=\frac{\lambda(L-l)}l\) and \(T=mL\omega^2\) for positive stretch.

blocks.title: Find the stretched length of a conical string
blocks.prompt: A mass of \(3\) kilograms moves in a horizontal circle, attached to an elastic string of natural length \(\frac{5}{3}\) metres and modulus \(\frac{125}{2}\,\mathrm N\). Its angular speed is \(\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{4}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Find the stretched length and radius. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
blocks.hint: Distinguish the natural length, stretched length and horizontal radius.
blocks.solution:
Inward and vertical equations give \(T=mL\omega^2\) and \(\cos\theta=\frac{g}{L\omega^2}\).

Equate tension to \(\frac{\lambda(L-l)}l\). Solving gives length \(\frac{8}{3}\) metres, above natural length.

The cosine is \(\frac{4}{5}\). The stretched length is \(\frac{8}{3}\) metres and radius is \(\frac{8}{5}\) metres.

blocks.html: Check both positive extension and a valid inclination after solving.

blocks.title: Find the stretched length of a conical string
blocks.prompt: A mass of \(5\) kilograms moves in a horizontal circle, attached to an elastic string of natural length \(\frac{7}{3}\) metres and modulus \(\frac{175}{2}\,\mathrm N\). Its angular speed is \(\frac{5 \sqrt{2}}{4}\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\). Find the stretched length and radius. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
blocks.hint: Distinguish the natural length, stretched length and horizontal radius.
blocks.solution:
Inward and vertical equations give \(T=mL\omega^2\) and \(\cos\theta=\frac{g}{L\omega^2}\).

Equate tension to \(\frac{\lambda(L-l)}l\). Solving gives length \(4\) metres, above natural length.

The cosine is \(\frac{4}{5}\). The stretched length is \(4\) metres and radius is \(\frac{12}{5}\) metres.

examples.question: A particle of mass \(2\) kilograms starts up a vertical circle from the bottom on a light string of length \(2\) metres, with speed \(\sqrt{10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the cosine of the angle from the downward vertical when it first stops, and the tension then. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
solution: Find the candidate turning point by setting \(v=0\) in the height energy equation.
The cosine there is \(\frac{3}{4}\), positive, so tension remains non-negative on the way there.
At the turning point the tension is \(15\,\mathrm N\). It does not lose the string constraint first.

examples.title: Find first loss of exterior contact
examples.question: A ball starts at the top of the outside of a fixed smooth sphere of radius \(2\) metres, with horizontal speed \(\frac{\sqrt{30}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the cosine of the angle from the upward vertical when it loses contact, and its exact speed. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
solution: Here inward is towards the centre. The radial equation is \(mg\cos\theta-N=\frac{mv^2}{r}\).
Energy gives \(v^2=u^2+2gr(1-\cos\theta)\). At loss of contact set \(N=0\).
The cosine is \(\frac{13}{18}\) and exact speed is \(\frac{\sqrt{130}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find first loss of exterior contact
examples.question: A ball starts at the top of the outside of a fixed smooth sphere of radius \(3\) metres, with horizontal speed \(\sqrt{15}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the cosine of the angle from the upward vertical when it loses contact, and its exact speed. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Energy gives \(v^2=u^2+2gr(1-\cos\theta)\). At loss of contact set \(N=0\).
The cosine is \(\frac{5}{6}\) and exact speed is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Compare the zero-speed and zero-tension boundaries
examples.question: A ball on a light string of length \(\frac{5}{2}\) metres has bottom speed \(\frac{5 \sqrt{6}}{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Decide whether it first turns with positive tension, reaches a zero-speed zero-tension boundary, loses tension at positive speed, or can complete the circle. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
solution: The dimensionless ratio \(\frac{u^2}{gr}\) is \(\frac{3}{2}\).
Compare this ratio with \(2\), the simultaneous horizontal boundary, and \(5\), the limiting complete-circle condition.
The turning cosine is positive, and the tension there is still positive. The first event is a turn. The relevant boundary radius has cosine \(\frac{1}{4}\) from the downward vertical.

examples.title: Check whether the circle is possible
examples.question: A ball on a taut light string of length \(\frac{4}{3}\) metres starts at the lowest point at speed \(2 \sqrt{15}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Can it complete the vertical circle with the string taut throughout? Give the squared speed the energy equation predicts at the top. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
solution: A taut string requires non-negative tension. The least tension is at the top for an orbit continuing without losses.
The top's energy-only prediction is \(v_{\rm top}^2=\frac{20}{3}\). Contact at the top needs at least \(\frac{40}{3}\).
The answer is no. The ball would need an outward string force by the top, so it cannot remain constrained throughout.

extraPractice.title: Locate the first slackening point
extraPractice.prompt: A ball starts at the bottom of a vertical circle on a light string of length \(3\) metres at speed \(\sqrt{105}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the cosine of its angle from the downward vertical and exact speed when tension first vanishes. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
extraPractice.hint: A string goes slack at zero tension, which need not be zero speed.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(v^2=u^2-2gr(1-\cos\theta)\) and \(T=m\left(\frac{v^2}{r}+g\cos\theta\right)\).

Tension decreases as the angle increases from the bottom along the ascent. Setting it to zero gives cosine \(- \frac{1}{2}\).

The speed there is \(\sqrt{15}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), positive, so the point is reached before a turning point.

sections.title: Which quantities change instantly when a peg catches the string?
sections.label: Carry the tangent speed
sections.intro: When the instantaneous new circle has the same tangent and ideal contact makes no tangential impulse, speed is unchanged. Radius and tension can change.

blocks.html: Use the remaining free string length as the new radius.

figure.alt: At the bottom B, the support lies directly above a peg and B. Two circular arcs have the same tangent at B.
figure.caption: A shorter free length gives a different inward acceleration even though the tangent speed at B is unchanged.

blocks.title: Track the velocity when a peg changes the circle
blocks.prompt: A ball of mass \(3\) kilograms on a taut string of length \(\frac{5}{2}\) metres crosses the bottom at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At that instant the string catches on a peg directly above the ball, leaving a new free length \(\frac{3}{2}\) metres. Assume the smooth instantaneous change preserves tangential speed. Find the tension immediately before and immediately after the catch. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
blocks.hint: Use the free length below the peg as the new radius. The change is in radial acceleration, not the depth of the ball at the instant.
blocks.solution:
The bottom velocity is horizontal and tangent to each of the two circles. Use the same speed and change the radius.

At the bottom the inward resultant is \(T-mg\). With the first radius the tension is \(\frac{366}{5}\,\mathrm N\).

With the smaller radius the tension increases to \(102\,\mathrm N\).

blocks.html: Do not re-use the old radius after the catch.

sections.title: Can the new circle be completed after the catch?
sections.label: Test the new top
sections.intro: After a smooth catch, use the common bottom state and the new circle height. Energy and the constraint supply separate checks.

blocks.html: Compare the energy-predicted speed at the new top with the minimum speed needed for non-negative tension.

blocks.title: Test the new circle after a peg changes the radius
blocks.prompt: A ball passes the bottom of a vertical circle with speed \(3 \sqrt{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Its initially taut string has length \(3\) metres. It catches a fixed peg directly above the ball and has free length \(\frac{6}{5}\) metres after the catch. Assume the tangent velocity is unchanged. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the predicted squared speed at the new top and decide whether the new full circle is possible.

fields.label: Predicted squared speed at the new top

blocks.hint: Test the new radius using the same bottom speed. An energy-only top speed is not enough to prove tension stays non-negative.
blocks.solution:
The new circle uses the shorter free length. Its top is \(\frac{12}{5}\) metres above the catch point.

The energy equation predicts squared speed \(6\) at the top. The string’s non-negative tension condition requires squared speed at least \(12\) there.

The predicted squared speed is \(6\). Therefore the complete new circle is not possible.

blocks.html: A successful old orbit does not prove the same force at the new radius.

sections.title: Which law applies at an instantaneous collision?
sections.label: Use the impact law first
sections.intro: An impact can change tangent speed abruptly. Use momentum in a direction with no external impulse and use restitution along the line of centres.

blocks.html: Find the immediate new velocities, then restart circular motion with the new speed.

blocks.title: Recalculate speed after a tangential impact
blocks.prompt: A ball of mass \(3\) kilograms on a taut string of length \(\frac{5}{2}\) metres strikes a stationary ball of mass \(\frac{3}{2}\) kilograms at the bottom of a vertical circle. It was moving at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and the direct horizontal impact has coefficient of restitution \(\frac{1}{3}\). Find the first ball’s immediate speed and subsequent tension at the bottom. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
blocks.hint: Energy need not be conserved during impact. Solve the impact first, then write the radial equation.
blocks.solution:
External support impulses have no horizontal component at the bottom. Conserve horizontal momentum and use the restitution relation along the line of centres.

The first ball leaves with speed \(\frac{10}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the second with speed \(\frac{16}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Apply the radial equation at the bottom with the first ball’s new speed. Its tension is \(\frac{130}{3}\,\mathrm N\).

blocks.html: Mechanical energy need not survive an inelastic impact.

sections.title: What happens after release along a horizontal tangent?
sections.label: Start free flight
sections.intro: The last tangent is the initial velocity of the free flight. Weight is the only force in the particle model after release.

blocks.html: Use the positive time from the vertical fall and multiply by horizontal speed.

blocks.title: Transfer tangent velocity into free flight
blocks.prompt: A ball loses its constraint at speed \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), moving right and horizontally. A level floor lies \(5\) metres below the release point. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the time to the floor and its horizontal range from release.
blocks.hint: Use the given tangent direction as the free-flight direction. After release only gravity determines acceleration.
blocks.solution:
The velocity immediately after release is tangent to the old motion. Its horizontal and vertical components are \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Use the free-flight vertical equation with displacement \(-5\) metres. The positive time is \(1\) seconds.

The horizontal range is \(6\) metres with unchanged horizontal velocity.

blocks.html: Use the two initial components in the separate projectile equations, and select the positive event time.
